newsitem.title: UK: Analysts see Yeltsin Duma address as Norilsk key.
newsitem.headline: Analysts see Yeltsin Duma address as Norilsk key.

text.p: Significant developments at Russia's strike-threatened Norilsk metals complex may have to wait until after Russian President Boris Yeltsin addresses parliament on Thursday, analysts said.
"Yeltsin has to address national problems, and wage arrears (as at Norilsk) are a national problem," said Andy Smith, precious metals analyst at Union Bank of Switzerland said on Monday.
Around 50,000 workers at the Siberian plant voted at the weekend to strike if management failed to settle a dispute over wage arrears within 10 days.
A management spokesman at Norilsk, a key producer of nickel and platinum group metals, said on Monday morning the deadline was impossible.
London Metal Exchange nickel prices on Monday hit a nine-month high of $8,300 a tonne, against Friday's close of $8,070.

Platinum was indicated around $391.00 an ounce and palladium at $151.00 after profit-taking reduced the former from the $406.00 touched briefly on Friday. At the beginning of the year these metals were valued at $369.00 and $120.75 respectively.
Smith said Yeltsin's address on March 6 would "help the fog clear" around the leadership vacuum that had developed since the premier's illness.
"It might defuse the situation if things are seen to be happening at the centre," he said.

Another key issue would be a Yeltsin reshuffle at head of deparment level, which might help to kick start resolution of issues such as Norilsk's tax and wage arrears and -- another factor for platinum metals -- the opening of export negotiations.
There has been no sign of talks beginning between Russia's platinum group metal (PGM) export agency and Japan's importing trade houses, Russia's main PGM customer.
Market analyst Tony Warwick-Ching at CRU International labelled the platinum and palladium markets "mysterious".
"There is no sign of an underlying shortage in either platinum or palladium," he said, noting that Japanese imports for January -- largely bought from the dealer market -- were "well up to average".
On the other hand, he said, investment funds had made it well known that they were buying into palladium, normally an illiquid market that attracts little speculative interest.
Russian deliveries of both metals to the U.S. and Switzerland were well above normal monthly levels at the end of last year, he said.
There were "strains" between different grades of material through tight availability, especially of sponge grade palladium, which is the form favoured for moist industrial applications, he said.
Last week sponge grade palladium was commanding premiums of up to $8 compared with a more usual $1 over ingot.
Warwick-Ching said it was difficult to see a long stoppage at Norilsk at this time of year.
Even if the complex was idled, the production pipeline from mine to refined product was so long that it would be months before supply was affected.
"There is the feeling that they have plenty of palladium in stock but they might not be so comfortable with platinum," he said.
--Brian Spoors, London Newsroom +44 171 542 8058
